articles.title: US appoints new cybersecurity chief after series of tech failures
articles.summary: Appointee Kirsten Davies says US has the chance to ‘dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come’.
articles.body:
The White House has fired the United States’s cybersecurity chief and appointed a replacement, days after widespread outages disrupted air travel, banking and national security systems.

Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Department of Defense, was appointed on Thursday to replace Sean Cairncross, who was reportedly sacked.

President Donald Trump’s administration has come under scrutiny over its handling of outages that hit Microsoft, the air industry and banks.

A communications failure disrupted air traffic late last week, grounding all flights in the US for about four hours and causing more than 10,000 flights to be cancelled . The disruption is expected to have cost travellers more than $1.9bn in lost time and expenses, according to the Anderson Economic Group.

Microsoft has apologised after governments, businesses and individuals around the world were affected as server failures caused outages of email and websites.

This week, bank customers across the US reported problems accessing services after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted transactions involving other banks.

The incidents have renewed questions about the vulnerabilities of critical infrastructure, most of which depends on modern-day technology.

“Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected,” Davies said in a social media post.

“Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernise and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future. Under President Trump’s leadership we will have a more secure, resilient; and supercharged technological future.”

US officials have said the outages were not caused by a cyberattack.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Wednesday that the disruptions were likely due to organisations using artificial intelligence to fix security flaws and carry out maintenance updates.

articles.title: A Texas woman alleged her three brothers divided gold and silver coins from their mother's safe while she was in hospice; a jury valued the coins at $630,603, and a November 19 appeals court restored its damages finding
articles.summary: A Texas appeals court has overturned a lower court ruling and restored a jury's $630,603 damages award in a family dispute that lasted nearly a decade.
articles.body: A Texas appeals court has overturned a lower court ruling and restored a jury's $630,603 damages award in a family dispute that lasted nearly a decade. The case involved gold and silver coins removed from a dying mother's home safe. In a memorandum opinion issued on November 19, 2026, Justice Jay Wright of the Ninth Court of Appeals in Beaumont ruled in favour of Cynthia Ann Reeves, the daughter and independent executor of Yolanda M. Coco's estate. The decision overturns a judgment by County Court at Law No. 1 in Jefferson County, Texas. That court had previously cancelled the jury's compensation award against Reeves's three brothers: Charles X. Sanchez, James O. Sanchez, and Oscar I. Sanchez Jr.Family meeting and midnight removalAccording to court records published by Justia, Yolanda M. Coco entered hospice care on July 5, 2016. She began taking morphine to manage her pain before she died on November 12, 2016. Soon after she entered hospice care, her children held a family meeting to discuss her finances. During the trial, Reeves testified that her three brothers voted to divide their mother's collection of gold and silver coins. She said she objected because Coco was still alive and might need the money and valuables to pay for her care. Another sister, Diana, did not take part in the vote. Reeves claimed that on July 31, 2016, her three brothers opened Coco's home safe and divided the coins without telling her. During the trial, the jury watched videos recorded by the brothers showing the coins after they had been divided. Reeves testified that neither she nor Diana received any of the precious metals at that time. Diana also testified that she opposed dividing the coins because their mother needed them to support herself. According to Diana's testimony, Charles Sanchez later told her, after their mother's death, that he had divided the coins among the brothers. He also said he was keeping her share until she decided which side of the family dispute she supported.Brothers claim mother gave permissionThe brothers denied taking the coins without permission. During the trial, James Sanchez testified that he had suggested dividing the contents of the safe into five equal shares at the July family meeting. He said this would allow each sibling to help pay for Coco's care and send money to Reeves whenever needed. James told the court that Coco called him on July 30, 2016. He said she asked him to bring Charles and remove the gold and silver from her safe, telling him, "[i]t's yours." According to his testimony, he and Charles drove from Dallas and reached Coco's home at around 2 a.m. on July 31. He said Coco repeated that the coins were "'yours and your bothers.'"Charles Sanchez also testified that Coco gave them permission to take the coins. He said she gave Oscar the safe's key and combination. However, he admitted that after the earlier family vote, Coco had first said she did not want the coins divided that day. He claimed she later called them and told them to collect the items. After the coins were removed, Reeves discovered in November 2016 that the safe was empty. She then obtained a court order requiring the coins to be returned for safekeeping. Court records showed that in late September and early October 2017, Charles returned 500 one-ounce Silver American Eagle coins on his own behalf. He also returned 500 Silver Canadian Maples, 320 Silver American Eagle coins, and four one-ounce Gold American Eagle coins on James's behalf. Both brothers testified that they had already sold some of the coins. Charles estimated that he had sold his share for about $50,000.Invoices and market charts at centre of appealThe main issue in the appeal was whether the jury had enough evidence to work out the fair market value of the coins when they were taken. During the trial, Reeves presented purchase invoices and order forms showing that Coco had spent $759,536 on precious metals between January 2011 and May 2014. Most of the purchases were made through US Rare Coin and Bullion Reserve. The records listed thousands of one-ounce American Silver Eagles, Canadian Silver Maples, American Gold Eagles, Liberty of Congress coins, and 2014 American Gold Buffalo coins.Reeves also presented daily historical charts showing gold and silver prices throughout 2016. The trial court allowed these charts into evidence, and the defence did not object to them. A first cousin, Raul Morales Jr., also testified that conversations with family members had led him to believe there was "probably close to $500,000" worth of gold and silver in the safe. After the jury awarded $630,603 in damages for the conversion of the coins, the brothers asked the Jefferson County trial judge to set aside the verdict. Their lawyers argued that no witness had done the mathematical calculations in front of the jury or directly stated the exact market value of the coins on July 31 or November 12, 2016. The trial court accepted this argument, cancelled the damages award, and ruled that the brothers did not have to pay anything.Ninth Court of Appeals reverses lower rulingIn its November 19 opinion, the Ninth Court of Appeals rejected the trial court's decision. It found that Reeves had presented more than a small amount of legally acceptable evidence to support the jury's $630,603 valuation. Reeves's lawyers argued that an expert witness was not needed in an estate conversion case. They said the jury could use the number of coins listed in Coco's purchase invoices and multiply those amounts by the daily gold and silver market prices for 2016. Those price charts had already been admitted into evidence without any objection from the defence. The appeals court agreed that the trial court had made a mistake by cancelling the jury's award. It reversed the judgment that had ruled in favour of the brothers and sent the case back to Jefferson County Court at Law No. 1 for further proceedings in line with its opinion.You use AI every day. articles.title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.summary: Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
articles.body:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday and Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".

Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.

He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," he said.

A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.

"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.

The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.

At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.

This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland and in July a cruise missile also landed in Poland.

articles.title: US targets Iran’s ship-to-ship transfers: Can Tehran break the blockade?
articles.summary: CENTCOM declares vessels bypassing the Iran blockade could be stopped, boarded or even seized by US forces.
articles.body:
The United States military has tightened its naval blockade of Iran , warning that vessels receiving Iranian cargo through ship-to-ship transfers will face military action.

US Central Command (CENTCOM), in an advisory on Wednesday, said ships receiving cargo from vessels loaded at Iranian ports or along the country’s coastline could be considered to be “evading the blockade”.

The move is aimed at closing a potential loophole that has allowed some Iranian petroleum products to reach international markets, despite Washington’s blockade of Iranian ports and oil exports since mid-July.

It comes as Tehran seeks ways to revive its oil exports, with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) repeatedly warning of retaliation against attacks on Iranian vessels.

Analysts say that while Iran is unlikely to break the blockade militarily, it could seek to make its enforcement politically and economically costly for Washington, raising the risk of a wider regional confrontation.

“This is potentially one of the most dangerous escalation scenarios we have seen in recent weeks,” Andreas Krieg, associate professor in Security Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.

So, can Iran circumvent the blockade, and could attempts to do so trigger a wider confrontation?

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Wednesday that ships receiving cargo from vessels loaded at Iranian ports or along the country’s coastline could be considered to be evading the blockade.

“Any ship that receives cargo via a ship-to-ship transfer with a vessel subject to the blockade and carrying cargo loaded at an Iranian port or coastline may be considered to be evading the blockade, even if it has not entered Iranian ports or the Iranian coastline,” CENTCOM said.

“Such ships may be stopped, boarded, diverted, captured, or directed to proceed to the Iranian port where the cargo originated.”

CENTCOM also warned that ships failing to comply with its orders could face enforcement action, including the use of force.

Washington initially imposed the blockade on April 13, lifted it in June following an understanding with Tehran, and reinstated it on July 14 after the agreement collapsed.

Iranian authorities have yet to issue a direct response to CENTCOM’s announcement, but Tehran has repeatedly warned against US efforts to restrict its trade.

An article published by Iran’s semi-official state outlet Fars News Agency on Wednesday proposed sending a group of oil tankers through the blockade while threatening retaliation against regional energy infrastructure if US forces intervened.

“To break the naval blockade, Iran can move a group of oil tankers to break out of the blockade,” the commentary said.

It suggested that any attack or obstruction could prompt Iran to target energy infrastructure in the region, “especially UAE oil”.

Earlier this month, IRGC spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebi rejected Washington’s ability to impose a comprehensive economic blockade on Iran.

“America can never achieve the type of economic blockade it’s after, whichever iteration it takes,” Mohebi said, according to Fars.

He also warned that Iran would retaliate if US forces attacked its vessels. “Naturally, in a war, they might hit one of our vessels. But we’ll hit harder,” he said.

Iran has managed to bypass parts of the blockade, but restoring large-scale crude exports presents a much greater challenge.

Before the US-Israeli war began in February, Iran exported roughly 1.5 million to 2 million barrels of crude oil per day, with China purchasing the vast majority of its shipments.

In October, Reuters news agency reported that at least eight tankers carrying Iranian liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) had left the Gulf of Oman since July, citing shipping intelligence and security sources. Another vessel delivered jet fuel to Myanmar in September, it said.

On Thursday, Reuters, citing maritime monitoring service TankerTrackers.com, reported that a vessel was loading Iranian crude through a ship-to-ship transfer in the Gulf.

If the shipment reaches its destination, it could become the first successful crude export since Washington reinstated the blockade in July, it added. There was no confirmation from Iranian authorities on this development.

Nevertheless, academic Krieg says Iran lacks the military capabilities to challenge the blockade directly.

“Iran can circumvent parts of the blockade, but it cannot break it militarily in any sustainable way. The Americans possess overwhelming naval superiority,” he warned.

“However, policing every shipment, intermediary and ship-to-ship transfer is considerably more complicated than stopping tankers leaving Iranian ports.”

Krieg said Gulf-based commercial networks have also facilitated Iranian oil exports, including through ship-to-ship transfers, although the extent of official government involvement remains unclear.

Washington’s latest restrictions could therefore create tensions with Gulf partners whose commercial interests do not necessarily align with US sanctions policy.

“I think Iran’s objective would be less about physically defeating the blockade than making its enforcement politically and economically unsustainable,” Krieg said.

“Sending tankers to challenge American forces could be designed to create a confrontation rather than simply deliver oil. But commentary in Fars should not be mistaken for an authorised operational plan.”

What would it mean for the conflict and the bigger picture?

The tightened blockade raises the prospect of further military confrontation between Washington and Tehran, particularly if Iranian tankers attempt to defy US restrictions.

Krieg warned that an American attack on an Iranian vessel could trigger retaliation against Gulf energy infrastructure, potentially drawing neighbouring countries deeper into the conflict.

“A confrontation involving Iranian tankers would introduce another threshold, particularly if American forces destroyed a vessel or caused substantial casualties,” he added.

Iran could respond by targeting Gulf energy infrastructure, seeking to demonstrate that its neighbours cannot continue exporting oil while Tehran remains cut off from international markets, Krieg noted.

“Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb would become interconnected fronts in an attempt to restore the balance of economic pain,” the academic said, referring to the Middle East’s two most vital straits.

Before the war, about 20 percent of the world’s oil and roughly one-fifth of global liquefied natural gas trade passed through the Strait of Hormuz, making it one of the world’s most important energy chokepoints. Another 5 percent of global energy transits through the Bab el-Mandeb, which connects the Red Sea to the Arabian Sea.

In retaliation for the war, Iran has de facto closed the Strait of Hormuz, severely reducing shipping traffic in the key waterway. And Tehran has repeatedly warned that the Houthis, its allies in Yemen, could similarly lock down the Bab el-Mandeb.

However, Krieg warned that such a strategy could backfire by alienating Gulf governments currently pushing Washington to avoid another major offensive.

“The fundamental contradiction is that Washington believes the blockade is working, while Tehran is approaching a point where the status quo is becoming economically intolerable,” he said.

“The more successful the blockade becomes, the greater Iran’s incentive to escalate rather than continue absorbing the costs.”

Despite the risks, Krieg believes both sides would still prefer a negotiated settlement. But without meaningful economic concessions, Tehran could increasingly resort to military action to challenge the blockade.

“The danger is that an operation intended to test American resolve becomes the trigger for another full-scale regional war,” Krieg said.

articles.title: What does the ICJ’s Rohingya genocide ruling mean for Gaza?
articles.summary: The case sets a precedent for establishing a state’s intent to commit genocide beyond explicitly written orders.
articles.body:
After seven years of deliberations and investigations, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its minority Rohingya population.

Thursday’s ruling by the United Nations’ top court in The Hague has been viewed as historic, the first genocide verdict it has handed down since it was established in 1945.

For the majority-Muslim Rohingya – 1.2 million of whom are languishing in cramped refugee camps in Bangladesh while more than 500,000 remain trapped and targeted in Myanmar – it marked vindication and international recognition of their suffering following decades of persecution, torture and killings at the hands of the Myanmar military and non-Rohingya rebel groups in their home state of Rakhine.

This judgement has given hope to other persecuted populations around the world. It now sets a precedent to establish a government’s intent to commit genocide – a difficult aspect of such cases.

Experts say the verdict has strong implications for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over its war on Gaza, which is one of those pending at the ICJ.

Just as Rohingya people celebrated and cried tears of joy when the court’s president pronounced a genocide ruling three hours into his readout of the verdict, many are wondering if this is a sign that Palestinians, too, will one day be able to do the same.

“This judgement will not decide the Gaza case,” Palestinian political analyst Ahmed Najar, however, told Al Jazeera. “But it may determine the legal lens through which Gaza is eventually judged.”

What is South Africa’s case against Israel?

On December 29, 2023, three months into Israel’s war on Gaza, South Africa filed an application against Israel at the Hague court, alleging that Israel was – and is – committing genocide against the Palestinian people living there.

Pretoria requested that the ICJ first approve emergency measures to protect civilians by immediately ordering Israel to suspend its military operations.

In two days of hearings in January 2024, the ICJ ruled that it is “plausible” that Israel’s actions could amount to genocide and ordered provisional measures requesting it “take all measures” to prevent the crime, despite Israel’s arguments that it was acting in self-defence following the deadly Hamas-led attacks on army outposts and villages in southern Israel on October 7, 2023, which resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people.

In March 2024, after South Africa had requested additional measures in light of Israel’s continued mass killings in Gaza, the court ordered Israel to ensure that food enters the enclave, finding that Palestinians in Gaza were facing famine and starvation.

In a third order in May that year, the ICJ ordered Israel to halt a deadly ground invasion in Rafah.

Israel did not comply with any of these orders, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have concluded.

At the time of the hearings in January 2024, some 23,000 people – including 10,000 children- had been killed in Gaza.

As of now, close to 75,000 people have been killed in Gaza, including an estimated 21,000 children. That does not include the thousands of people who are still missing and presumed dead under the rubble.

At least 1,662 people have been killed since an October 2025 US-brokered ceasefire agreement was announced between Israel and Hamas.

A verdict on whether Israel is committing genocide is expected to take several years as the two parties must submit written arguments and counterarguments. South Africa’s next submission will be in November 2027.

How is the Gaza case similar to The Gambia’s Myanmar case?

For both the Rohingya and Palestinians in Gaza, legal proceedings have offered little immediate solace: tent camps are being washed away amid intense storms for both refugee communities. Civilians are also still being killed – by continuing Israeli strikes on Gaza, most recently on the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza, and by violence against Rohingya in Myanmar from both military and rebel groups.

The two cases have important legal parallels.

The Gambia accused Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya in November 2019.

That was two years after the Tatmadaw, Myanmar’s feared military, first began “clearance operations” that it claimed were a response to attacks on police posts by the rebel Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, which is fighting for Rohingya independence.

Myanmar denied committing crimes against civilians despite photos, videos and satellite images which showed mass killings and razed Rohingya villages, and despite gruelling accounts of torture and rape from thousands of survivors, as well as hate speech spread by senior Tatmadaw commanders.

On Thursday, nine of the ICJ’s 15-judge panel on the Rohingya case ruled that the “only reasonable inference” to be made from the evidence of widespread atrocities in Myanmar was that indeed, genocide had been committed.

The court said Myanmar had knowingly allowed civilian militias to participate in targeting Rohingya, failed to investigate or punish culpable commanders, acted with “intent” to destroy the group and prevent births, and violated provisional measures earlier issued in 2020 to preserve evidence.

“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.

It ordered that Myanmar provide reparations and restitution by ensuring the safe return of Rohingya people to their lands, replacing damaged property and compensating those affected, accounting for missing people, reuniting families and ensuring dignified burials, providing medical and trauma care, and importantly, ensuring that such violations never happen again.

Such imagery and testimonies have also been abundant in Gaza, where 2.1m people are currently concentrated in a 128sq km area (35 percent of Gaza) behind Israel’s so-called “Yellow Line”. Israel’s far-right officials have also made numerous statements debasing Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

In 2025, the Al Jazeera Investigative Unit’s feature documentary, GAZA, also exposed Israeli war crimes through the use of videos and photographs posted online by Israeli soldiers themselves.

The court’s acceptance of evidence in the Rohingya case beyond just explicit, written orders from senior military figures has led observers to conclude that it could take a similar view in relation to the war on Gaza.

Like Myanmar, Israel has claimed a right to self-defence, and says it is targeting Hamas, rather than civilians, despite the majority of casualties being women and children.

In its ruling against Myanmar, the court has demonstrated that intent to commit genocide can be inferred from cumulative patterns, Najar said. “The court must assess the evidence concerning Gaza independently, but [this ruling] provides South Africa with a much clearer legal road map,” he said.

At the centre of the Myanmar case lay the central question that defined the past quarter-century: whether a state may destroy a people so long as it describes that brutality as “counterterrorism”, Anas Mustapha of the UK-based advocacy organisation, CAGE International, said.

“Today, for the first time, a court has refused to accept that defence, and Myanmar has been held to account for a genocide it carried out in that language,” he noted, adding that the US and other colonial Western nations provided the templates used against the Rohingya and Palestinians.

“The governments that wrote the language, from the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq to the genocide in Gaza, have so far escaped any such reckoning.”

Why has the ICJ so rarely found genocide?

Genocide – specifically the intent to commit it – is much harder to prove than war crimes or crimes against humanity.

The 1948 Genocide Convention defines it as crimes committed “with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group”.

In addition to intent, five prohibited acts prove genocide has been committed: killing members of the group, causing them serious bodily or mental harm, creating conditions calculated to destroy them, preventing births, or forcibly transferring children to other groups. Myanmar was convicted on four of those.

The ICJ can only rule on matters between states, not individuals. To conclusively prove genocide, the prosecuting party must show intent by the defending state, not just some individuals within it. That’s where prior cases have fallen apart.

For example, in 2007, the ICJ ruled that Serbia did not commit genocide, but that it violated the Convention by failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops in Srebrenica. This was despite UN tribunals finding individual actors in the case culpable of genocide.

However, since 2007, the current ICJ has proven much more flexible in its approach by ruling that genocide can exist even when the stated aim is self-defence, said Triestino Mariniello, a professor of law at Liverpool John Moores University in the UK.

“The contexts are different, of course, but this can also likely be applied exactly to Gaza where there’s widespread and systemic violations,” he said. “If the court had concluded differently, we would have known there was no case for South Africa, but this paves the way.”

The ruling may affect states that could be held accountable as accessories to Israel’s crimes.

The US, Israel’s staunchest ally, said it was watching closely ahead of the verdict. Washington has already sanctioned the International Criminal Court (ICC) and its judges because of arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. There are fears Washington will also now target the ICJ following its Myanmar ruling.

While neither the US nor Israel are parties to the ICC, they are automatically members of the ICJ as members of the United Nations.

Ahead of the Rohingya verdict, Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, accused South African lawyer and Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay, who acted as a jurist on the case, of “tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar”.

He claimed she intended to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians”.

Meanwhile, Germany, Israel’s strongest ally in Europe, actually joined several other countries in supporting The Gambia’s case against Myanmar, asking the court to not only look at evidence of killings, but also at the treatment of children, sexual violence and forced displacements. All of these apply to the catastrophe in Gaza, observers say.

In March 2024, Nicaragua sued Germany at the ICJ for alleged breaches of its international obligations under the Genocide Convention and international humanitarian law over continued arms supplies to Israel. Proceedings in that are continuing.

articles.title: Finchley teacher misses sentencing for indecent assault on pupils
articles.summary: A warrant is issued for the arrest of Sally-Anne Bowen, who was granted bail after a guilty verdict.
articles.body:
A judge has issued a warrant for the arrest of a teacher convicted of sexually abusing two pupils at an all-boys school in the late 1980s after she failed to turn up for her sentencing hearing.

Sally-Anne Bowen was in her 20s when she had sex with one pupil up to 30 times and kissed a second boy while the pupils were aged about 14 or 15.

Her trial heard the chemistry teacher wore short tight skirts and flirted in class, with one former pupil comparing her behaviour to "a Sabrina Carpenter video".

After being convicted earlier this year of seven counts of indecent assault, the 65-year-old was granted bail and was due to be sentenced at Harrow Crown Court on Friday.

But Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, did not turn up to court, and Judge Karim Ezzat issued an arrest warrant.

Neelam Gomersall, prosecuting, said there was "no evidence" that Bowen could not attend the sentencing, and information from her partner was "suggestive of refusal rather than inability" to attend.

Defence barrister Mark Kimsey said his client had been in contact with solicitors and had engaged with a pre-sentence report, adding there had been "concerns as to her welfare due to the content of the messages" from her.

articles.title: GTA 6 locations based on real places: 10 Florida landmarks and neighbourhoods recreated with fictional names in Leonida
articles.summary: Grand Theft Auto 6 takes players to Leonida, a fictional US state inspired by Florida, where familiar real-world locations have been recreated with new
articles.body: Grand Theft Auto 6 takes players to Leonida, a fictional US state inspired by Florida, where familiar real-world locations have been recreated with new names and identities. From Miami's South Beach, reimagined as Ocean Beach, to the Everglades-inspired Grassrivers and the island landscapes of the Leonida Keys, the game draws heavily on Florida's geography, architecture and natural environments. Other recognisable references include Little Havana, Miami International Airport, PortMiami and the Apalachicola National Forest. Here are 10 real places in Florida that have inspired GTA 6 locations.GTA 6 locations: From Miami's South Beach to the EvergladesMiami's South Beach becomes Ocean BeachThe stretch of coastline known for its Art Deco buildings, busy pavements and beachside activity has a counterpart in GTA 6 called Ocean Beach. It takes inspiration from South Beach and Ocean Drive in Miami, a connection confirmed on Rockstar's official website.Ocean Drive is one of the most recognisable parts of Miami's waterfront. Its architecture, hotels and restaurants have made the area a familiar feature of the city. In Leonida, Rockstar retains the coastal identity while giving the location a fictional name.Little Havana as Little CubaMiami's Little Havana has been reimagined as Little Cuba in the game. Rockstar has confirmed the connection through its official website, making it one of the more clearly established geographical references in Leonida.The real neighbourhood is closely associated with Cuban-American culture. Calle Ocho, its best-known street, brings together restaurants, bakeries, cigar shops, art galleries and small businesses that have served the community for generations. Coffee windows known as ventanitas are also a familiar part of the area's street life.Little Havana has received recognition from the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which designated it a National Treasure. Its importance goes beyond tourism, with the neighbourhood serving as a centre of Cuban-American cultural life in Miami.Miami-Dade County inspires Vice-Dale CountyRockstar has also borrowed from Florida's administrative geography. Miami-Dade County, which includes Miami and several surrounding communities, has a fictional equivalent in GTA 6 called Vice-Dale County.The name follows a familiar approach used throughout the Grand Theft Auto series. Rather than reproduce the real location exactly, the developer changes parts of its name while keeping enough of the original reference recognisable.Here, Miami becomes Vice, a reference to Vice City, while Dade is changed to Dale.Kaseya Center appears as Sahara ArenaThe Miami Heat's home venue has a counterpart in GTA 6 named Sahara Arena. The connection is based on footage from the game's first trailer, which offered viewers a look at a building resembling the Kaseya Center.Located in downtown Miami, the Kaseya Center is a major sports and entertainment venue. It hosts Miami Heat basketball games as well as concerts and other large events.Unlike Ocean Beach and Little Cuba, this particular reference is drawn from trailer footage rather than a direct listing on Rockstar's official website.Apalachicola National Forest as Mount Kalaga National ParkLocated near Leonida's northern border, Mount Kalaga National Park brings a different kind of landscape to GTA 6. Rather than the beaches and busy streets associated with Vice City, this part of the fictional state takes inspiration from the wooded wilderness of North Florida, particularly the Apalachicola National Forest.The real forest covers approximately 567,742 acres and is known for its longleaf pine woodlands, sandy trails, wetlands and winding waterways. Its landscape includes remote dirt roads and rivers darkened by tannins from surrounding vegetation. Florida has no substantial mountain ranges, making its northern forests a more fitting reference for Rockstar's rugged backcountry setting.Miami International Airport gets a Vice City counterpartAir travel also has a familiar presence in Leonida. Miami International Airport, one of Florida's busiest aviation hubs, is represented by Vice City International Airport.The connection comes from Rockstar's trailer footage, which includes scenes showing an airport resembling its real-world counterpart. The naming follows the same pattern used for several other locations, replacing Miami with Vice City.Miami International Airport is a major gateway for domestic and international travellers, particularly those travelling between the United States, Latin America and the Caribbean. Its position in South Florida makes it a natural reference for a game drawing so heavily on the region.PortMiami is recreated as Port Vice CityThe waterfront infrastructure of Miami has also influenced the game's setting. PortMiami appears to have inspired Port Vice City, a location shown in the trailers.The real port occupies Dodge Island in Biscayne Bay, close to Fisher Island and Star Island. It is an important part of Miami's maritime landscape, with cruise terminals and cargo facilities forming a large part of its operations.Its island setting is one of the geographical details that makes the comparison interesting. The port is not simply another building in the city's skyline but an extensive waterfront area with a distinct position within Miami's coastal geography.Florida Keys inspire the Leonida KeysSouth of mainland Florida, the chain of islands known as the Florida Keys provides another reference for GTA 6. Rockstar's official website identifies the Leonida Keys as the game's version of the real archipelago.Florida is replaced with Leonida, while the word Keys remains unchanged. The actual Florida Keys are known for their island communities, coastal roads and access to the surrounding waters. The region also includes natural areas such as Bahia Honda State Park and Dagny Johnson Key Largo Hammock Botanical State Park.The Everglades become GrassriversOne of Florida's most distinctive natural environments has been given a different identity in GTA 6. The Everglades appear in the game as Grassrivers, a region of Leonida that Rockstar describes on its official website as a major natural feature of the fictional state.The real Everglades is a vast wetland system in southern Florida. Often described as a slow-moving river of grass, its shallow freshwater flows south from Lake Okeechobee towards the Gulf of Mexico.Its landscape is far from uniform. Sawgrass marshes cover extensive areas, while cypress forests, mangroves and elevated hardwood habitats known as hammocks form other parts of the ecosystem. The ground beneath much of the region consists of limestone and marl, generally covered by layers of organic material and some sand.Miami's Wynwood art as StockyardStockyard is one of the locations featured in Rockstar Games' upcoming title Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), set in the fictional state of Leonida. As players explore Vice City and its surrounding areas, Stockyard adds another layer to the game's detailed urban landscape. articles.title: Drones keep eye on Chilika lake as villagers defy cyclone safety advisory
articles.summary: Police deploy drones to monitor Chilika Lake during cyclone Akvan, spotting illegal fishing and boat rides as villagers ignore safety advisories.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: Amid incessant rain under the influence of cyclone Akvan, Khurda district police on Friday pressed drones into service to keep a close watch on Chilika lake and prevent unauthorised boat movement and fishing activities.Police said aerial surveillance was adopted after several villagers living close to the lake were allegedly found ignoring the govt’s safety advisory and restrictions imposed in view of the rough weather.SP (Khurda) Smit Parmar said the drones proved effective in detecting fishermen attempting to venture into the choppy waters despite the administration’s ban on fishing and boat movement. Police said the surveillance also spotted some villagers taking boat rides in the lake, putting their lives at risk.Police patrol teams were deployed in vulnerable villages near Chilika to warn residents against entering the lake and ensure compliance with safety measures. However, officers said some residents resumed fishing or boating soon after patrol teams moved out of their areas.“It is not possible for us to remain round the clock in every village. We noticed that some people became careless once our patrol teams left. The drones helped us monitor larger stretches of the lake and quickly identify any unauthorised movement,” another police officer said.Police said teams on the ground were alerted whenever drones detected suspicious boat movement so that immediate steps could be taken to bring the occupants back to safety. The surveillance was being carried out particularly in areas where fishermen and people frequently used boats for livelihood and transportation.Police used public address systems, appealing to residents living along Chilika to strictly follow the administration’s advisory and avoid venturing into the lake until weather conditions improve. articles.title: Police officers guilty of misconduct over St Mellons fatal crash inquiry
articles.summary: PC Richard Hardwick and PC Lauren Livingstone faced allegations over their actions around a 2023 crash in St Mellons.
articles.body:
Two police officers who lied about carrying out missing person searches linked to a crash in which three people died have been found guilty at a police misconduct hearing.

PC Richard Hardwick and PC Lauren Livingstone faced gross misconduct allegations over their actions before a car carrying five people was found crashed two days later in a woodland in St Mellons, Cardiff, in 2023.

The hearing in Newport was told they were "dishonest" in official logs and to a senior officer by claiming searches of the homes of Eve Smith, who died, and Sophie Russon had been carried out.

Hardwick and Livingstone's punishment is expected to be heard on Friday afternoon.

Panel chairman Ian Arundale said Hardwick and Livingstone had deliberately misled a missing persons investigation, which may have compromised the investigation, and had undermined public trust in the police in a high-profile case.

Hardwick faced six allegations, including that he lied about searching the homes of crash victims Smith and Russon, and that he also lied to his supervising officer and the police watchdog.

Livingstone faced four allegations, including that she lied about searching the two houses, as well as making a dishonest entry on the log and lying to her supervising officer.

The police disciplinary hearing at Rodney Parade, which lasted four days, was told that both officers were part of the team assigned to look into reports that Eve Smith, Darcy Ross and Sophie Russon had gone missing after a night out on Friday 3 March 2023.

The three women were reported missing to Gwent Police on 4 March, but were not found until 30 hours after the initial contact by the families.

Five people were found in a car in a wooded area off the A48, 46 hours after the vehicle had crashed.

Three of the cars occupants, Eve Smith, Rafel Jeanne, and Darcy Ross had died, and two, Sophie Russon and Shane Loughlin, were seriously injured.

Hardwick and Livingstone went to Russon's home and then on to Smith's house, and as part of Gwent police's missing person policy were supposed to search the address to look for clues for what might have happened to them.

Hardwick wrote in the official log afterwards "premise search conducted" and told the police sergeant overseeing the case that the search at Russon's house had been carried out. He also said searches had happened when he spoke to the police watchdog, the IOPC, who later investigated.

This was in contrast to what Russon's father, Nathan, told the hearing, that the officers were at the house for a very short period and did not ask to search the bedroom.

Livingstone said she could not remember whether searches had taken place, but wrote what she agreed was a "poorly written" report in the official log, which the panel head heard was "deliberately vague" but suggested a search had taken place.

The panel found Hardwick and Livingstone had failed to conduct a search at Smith and Russon's homes.

Hardwick was found to have provided a false entry into the police log and had provided a dishonest statement when interviewed by the IOPC.

He had been found, in part, to have given a dishonest account of the search to his supervisor and found in part to have provided a dishonest account in a signed statement to the IOPC.

Livingstone was found to also have provided a false entry into the police log and to have had given a dishonest account of the search to her supervisor.

Panel chairman Ian Arundale said their behaviour had caused harm because of the impact on the family and had undermined public trust in the police in a case which resulted in significant levels of concern from the public.
